  "idea": {
    "Name": "bias_stiffness_hysteron_duality",
    "Title": "Bias–Stiffness Duality in Mechanical Hysteron Networks: From Threshold Collapse to Programmable Eight-Cycles",
    "Short Hypothesis": "A coupling spring acts on a bistable rotor through two inseparable geometric channels: a state-dependent bias that shifts the switching center, c_i = (gamma_up + gamma_down)/2, and a state-dependent curvature that shrinks the hysteresis half-width, h_i = (gamma_up - gamma_down)/2. For a spring attached at lever arm L, the bias should scale linearly with L while the curvature scales as L^2, so h_i(L) = h_i(0) - K_i L^2 and c_i(s_j,L) = c_i(0) + J_i(L) s_j. This single law should explain why pair_A thresholds collapse inward with mounting distance, why pair_B crossed springs produce much larger common-mode center shifts, and why network_C executes one ordered 8-state limit cycle rather than an arbitrary transition graph. The best test is pair_A, where L varies with all else fixed, combined with the topology change in pair_B and the ordered events in network_C; threshold shifts alone can always be absorbed into an arbitrary Preisach field, but the predicted width contraction and its L^2 scaling are not.",
    "Related Work": "Interacting-hysteron work has shown that serial mechanical hysterons can realize geometrically controlled antiferromagnetic-like interactions and finite-state-machine behavior (PNAS 2024), and that connected balloons can be described by Preisach hysterons whose transition graphs change under volume control (PRE 2024). Mechanical metamaterials have also been designed to count cycles and process sequences (PRL 2023). These studies treat interactions mainly as threshold shifts or targeted transition graphs. The proposed bias–stiffness duality is distinct: it derives both the center shift and the hysteresis-width contraction from the same spring-energy expansion, predicts a specific quadratic lever-arm law, and uses that law to predict the topology and amplitude phase diagram of a four-rotor mechanical automaton. It is not a trivial extension of Preisach modeling because it tests a geometric relation between two usually separate phenomenological parameters.",
    "Abstract": "Mechanical hysterons are bistable units whose switching thresholds can be shifted by coupling. Existing models usually represent coupling as a state-dependent bias, leaving the hysteresis width unchanged. We propose that a coupling spring necessarily produces two channels: a bias torque, linear in the spring's lever arm L, and a curvature term, quadratic in L, that lowers the barrier and contracts the hysteresis width. Expanding the spring energy for rotor angle theta_i gives U_c = const + tau_ij(L) s_j theta_i + (1/2) kappa_ij(L) theta_i^2 + ..., so the measured thresholds obey c_i(s_j,L) = c_i0 + J_i(L) s_j and h_i(L) = h_i0 - K_i(L), with K_i proportional to L^2 for a fixed pretension. We test this on supplied measurements: pair_A varies coupling attachment distance L from 0 to 4.731 cm; pair_B changes from parallel to crossed coupling; network_C supplies 16 ordered state events forming an eight-state cycle. The data already show the predicted pattern: for pair_A rotor 1, h falls from 7.2 to 4.6 cm while the center shift grows approximately linearly; rotor 2, with a -1.9 cm mounting offset, shows a stronger, apparently quadratic center shift. Crossed pair_B springs produce much larger common-mode shifts. We then build a four-hysteron race model and predict that reducing drive amplitude should truncate the 8-cycle into smaller subcycles, while reversing one coupling sign should reverse or split the cycle. The result would turn mechanical hysteresis from a threshold lookup table into a geometrically constrained finite-state machine.",
    "Experiments": "1. Calibration reanalysis: fit each spring's loading/unloading force-extension curve with F = k(x-x0) plus a small hysteretic offset. Quantify stiffness and friction; use only as priors because calibration samples are not exact installed springs. 2. Pair_A threshold decomposition: for every (rotor_i, direction, other_state, mount_l_cm), compute c=(gamma_up+gamma_down)/2 and h=(gamma_up-gamma_down)/2. Fit c_i(s_j,L)=c_i0+J_i(L)s_j and h_i(L)=h_i0-K_i L^2. Report R^2, leave-one-L-out prediction error, and whether rotor 1 is linear in L while rotor 2 is quadratic, as expected from its -1.9 cm offset. 3. Pair_B topology test: fit the same decomposition to the eight crossed-spring rows. Test the ordinal prediction that crossed coupling gives larger |J| and opposite sign relative to pair_A at comparable L; because only one L is available, treat this as a sign/magnitude test, not a precise curve fit. 4. Network_C race model: implement four hysterons with thresholds gamma_i^±(s)=c_i+sum_j J_ij s_j ± [h_i-sum_j K_ij]. Under monotone drive segments, flip the rotor whose threshold is crossed first. Because network_C connectivity and stop angles are unknown, infer only qualitative constraints from the observed 16-event sequence and event drive values. Use cycle edit distance and whether the observed 8-cycle is a stable periodic orbit. 5. Proposed inexpensive perturbation: on network_C vary one coupling attachment distance or swap one parallel/crossed pair, and vary drive amplitude. Predict a period-8 to period-4/2/1 phase diagram, with the highest positive events (5.8-5.9 cm) disappearing first as amplitude is reduced, and a cycle reversal or split when one coupling sign is reversed. Metrics: threshold prediction error in cm, event-order accuracy, cycle period, cycle edit distance, and phase-boundary location.",
    "Risk Factors and Limitations": "Network_C's full connectivity, stop angles, attachment coordinates, and drive reversal positions are unknown, so its quantitative prediction is weak. The supplied rows are figure-source measurements, not independent repetitions; there are no error bars for thresholds or events, and no timestamps. Calibration samples are not exact identities of installed springs. Pair_B has only one mounting distance, so topology and lever-arm effects are confounded. The small-angle, pairwise, quasistatic spring model may fail near stops or when springs go slack; rotor 2's nonlinear center shift may indicate such a regime. The observed 8-cycle could be protocol-dependent, and two repeated cycles are not enough to establish stability. The proposal is explanatory and conditional: failure of the L^2 width law or of the predicted amplitude truncation would falsify the dual-channel mechanism."
